# Introduction

This document guides you through our project on the association between social
media use and mental health outcomes (sleep, anxiety measured with the GAD-7,
and depression measured with the PHQ-9).

The project has four parts:

1. **Main analysis (adults):** correlations, regressions and platform
   comparisons in the *Social Media and Mental Health* dataset on Kaggle
   (*Social Media and Mental Health*, n.d.).
2. **Shiny app:** an interactive tool that shows what the adult data suggest for
   a chosen platform and amount of daily screen time.
3. **Extra: adolescents (HBSC):** the same kind of question in data from the
   Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study (HBSC study, n.d.).
4. **Extra: simulation check:** simulated data with known effects, used to
   check that our regression approach recovers them.

> **Note:** All results describe statistical associations, not causal effects,
> and are not a diagnosis.

All heavy code lives in `src/`. This document only calls one high-level
function per part and explains the results. Every function also saves its tables,
figures and a text report to a folder inside `outputs/`.

# Setup

Open `pips-project.Rproj` first, so that the working directory is the project
folder. The chunk below installs any missing packages.

```{r packages}
required_packages <- c(
  # main analysis, HBSC analysis, simulation, app
  "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "purrr", "stringr", "tibble", "readr",
  "broom", "car", "MASS", "sandwich", "lmtest", "shiny",
  # this document
  "knitr", "rmarkdown"
)
missing_packages <- setdiff(required_packages, rownames(installed.packages()))
if (length(missing_packages) > 0) install.packages(missing_packages)
```

Load the three analysis functions. Sourcing only defines the functions; nothing
runs yet.

```{r source-functions}
source("src/run_screen_time_analysis.R")
source("src/run_hbsc_analysis.R")
source("src/run_social_media_analysis.R")
```

# Main analysis: adults (Kaggle data)

## Data and methods

`data/alternative_dataset.csv` contains, per respondent, daily screen time
(hours), primary platform, sleep duration (hours), GAD-7 (0–21) and PHQ-9 (0–27),
plus further variables (age, gender, activity type, late-night usage, social
comparison trigger) that this analysis does not use.

`run_screen_time_analysis()` checks the input and then runs:

- **Spearman correlations** between daily screen time and each outcome, with
  Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction across the three tests.
- **Linear regressions** of each outcome on daily screen time and platform.
  Platforms with fewer than 30 respondents are set to missing, and the most
  common remaining platform is the reference group. Regression p-values and
  confidence intervals are conventional and not corrected for multiple testing.
- **Platform comparisons:** Kruskal–Wallis tests and pairwise Wilcoxon tests
  (BH-corrected).
- **Interaction tests:** nested-model F-tests of whether the screen-time slope
  differs by platform (BH across the three outcomes).

No age, gender or other covariates are included. Regression diagnostics are saved
to the output folder but not displayed here.

```{r main-analysis}
screen_results <- run_screen_time_analysis(
  data_path    = "data/alternative_dataset.csv",
  output_dir   = "outputs/screen_time",
  print_plots  = FALSE,
  verbose      = FALSE
)
```

# The Shiny app

The app uses the same models as the main analysis: for each outcome it fits
`outcome ~ daily screen time + platform`, with the most common platform as the
reference group and platforms with fewer than 30 respondents removed.

Users tick their platform(s) and set their daily screen time, and see predictions
with 95% confidence and prediction intervals, curves across screen time, and
model tables. If several platforms are ticked, the app shows the average of the
per-platform predictions, since each respondent in the data has one platform.

The chunk is not evaluated when knitting. Run it manually; it opens in a browser
window or the RStudio viewer. Press the stop button in the console before running
further chunks.

```{r app, eval=FALSE}
shiny::runApp("src")  # runs src/app.R
```

# Extra: adolescents (HBSC)

The raw HBSC file was too large for GitHub, so we reduced it to 33 variables and
180,397 participants: we kept only variables on mental health, physical health and
social media use, recoded the missing-value code 99 to `NA`, and excluded
participants with more than 2 missing answers.

`run_hbsc_analysis()` recodes the eight social media items `emcsocmed2` to
`emcsocmed9` from 1/2 to 0/1 and sums them into a score from 0 to 8 (only for
participants who answered all eight). It then relates this score to four outcomes
(`feellow`, `nervous`, `sleepdificulty`, `physact60`) with Spearman correlations
and unadjusted linear regressions, BH-adjusted across the four tests. Outcome
directions are explained in `data/hbsc_data_descriptions.pdf`.

```{r hbsc-analysis}
hbsc_results <- run_hbsc_analysis(
  data_path     = "data/hbsc_data.csv",
  output_folder = "outputs/hbsc",
  print_plots   = FALSE,
  verbose       = FALSE
)
```

```{r hbsc-correlations}
knitr::kable(hbsc_results$correlation_results, digits = 3)
```

```{r hbsc-regressions}
knitr::kable(hbsc_results$regression_results, digits = 3)
```

```{r hbsc-figures, fig.width=8, fig.height=5.5}
hbsc_results$plots$score_distribution
for (p in hbsc_results$plots$associations) print(p)
```

with the adult data. The two datasets measure different things in different

# Extra: simulation check

To check that our regression approach works, `run_social_media_analysis()`
simulates fictional data for `n` participants: daily time on five apps (correlated),
age and gender, and four outcomes with effects that we impose. It fits one
regression per outcome that includes all five apps, age and gender, with
Holm correction across the 20 app-by-outcome tests and an HC3 robust-standard-error
sensitivity analysis. The data and effects are fictional, so the simulation says
nothing about real effects.

```{r simulation}
sim_results <- run_social_media_analysis(
  n             = 500,
  seed          = 2026,
  output_folder = "outputs/simulation",
  print_plots   = FALSE,
  verbose       = FALSE
)
```

```{r sim-coefficients}
sim_effects <- sim_results$app_results[c("outcome", "app", "estimate", "conf.low",
                                         "conf.high", "p.value",
                                         "p_holm_all_app_tests")]
knitr::kable(sim_effects, digits = 3)
```

```{r sim-figures, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}
sim_results$plots$adjusted_coefficients
sim_results$plots$app_correlations
```

**Do the estimates recover the true effects?** The true per-hour effects are the
ones set inside `run_social_media_analysis()`. They are repeated below for
comparison.

```{r sim-recovery}
true_effects <- data.frame(
  outcome = rep(c("Depression", "Anxiety", "Sleep problems", "Physical activity"),
                each = 5),
  term = rep(c("snapchat_hours", "instagram_hours", "tiktok_hours",
               "facebook_hours", "pinterest_hours"), times = 4),
  true_effect = c(0.35, 0.45, 0.60, 0.15, 0.05,
                  0.40, 0.45, 0.55, 0.10, 0.05,
                  0.25, 0.40, 0.55, 0.10, 0.05,
                  -1.2, -1.5, -2.0, -0.5, -0.3)
)
recovery <- merge(sim_results$app_results[c("outcome", "term", "app", "estimate",
                                            "conf.low", "conf.high")],
                  true_effects, by = c("outcome", "term"))
recovery$ci_contains_truth <- recovery$conf.low <= recovery$true_effect &
  recovery$true_effect <= recovery$conf.high
knitr::kable(recovery[c("outcome", "app", "true_effect", "estimate", "conf.low",
                        "conf.high", "ci_contains_truth")], digits = 3)
```

**Interpretation.** *TODO: how many of the 20 intervals contain the true effect?
With 95% intervals we expect about one miss. Outcomes are rounded and bounded in
the simulation, so small deviations are expected.*

# Limitations

- All results are associations, not causal effects.
- The main analysis does not adjust for age, gender or other covariates.
- *TODO: state whether the Kaggle data are real survey data or synthetic, as
  described on the Kaggle page, and what that means for generalisability.*
- Measures are self-reported, and the adult and adolescent samples differ in
  population and measurement.
- The HBSC analysis does not incorporate survey weights or clustering.
